title: Experimental Design & Scope of Inference
subtitle: ClipSAT Printable Practice Suite (clipsat.org) • Topic 2.02 • 20 FRQs + 25 MCQs • Difficulty Progression • Cross-Lesson Synthesis

sections.heading: Part I — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Foundational Fluency (1–7)

questions.q: A researcher records the exercise habits and cholesterol levels of 500 people without intervening in their lifestyle. Identify whether this is an observational study or an experiment, and explain what type of conclusion (association or causation) it can support.
questions.answer: This is an observational study, since the researcher only records existing behavior without imposing any treatment. It can only support conclusions about association between exercise and cholesterol, not causation, since confounding variables (diet, genetics, age) could explain the relationship instead.
questions.explanation: This is an observational study, since the researcher only records existing behavior without imposing any treatment. It can only support conclusions about association between exercise and cholesterol, not causation, since confounding variables (diet, genetics, age) could explain the relationship instead.

questions.q: A researcher randomly assigns 200 volunteers to either an exercise program or a no-exercise control group, then measures cholesterol after 6 months. Identify this design, and explain why it can support a causal conclusion.
questions.answer: This is an experiment, since the researcher actively assigns a treatment (exercise program). Random assignment balances out confounding variables between the two groups on average, so any significant difference in cholesterol can be attributed to the exercise program itself, supporting a causal conclusion.
questions.explanation: This is an experiment, since the researcher actively assigns a treatment (exercise program). Random assignment balances out confounding variables between the two groups on average, so any significant difference in cholesterol can be attributed to the exercise program itself, supporting a causal conclusion.

questions.q: State the three key principles of a well-designed experiment (sometimes remembered as RRC: Random assignment, Replication, Control of confounding variables), and briefly explain the purpose of each.
questions.target: The three principles of experimental design (RRCB)
questions.answer: Random assignment: randomly assigning subjects to treatment groups balances out lurking variables between groups. Replication: using enough subjects per treatment group reduces the role of chance variation, making real treatment effects easier to detect. Control: keeping other variables constant across groups (e.g. a comparison/control group, placebo, or blinding) isolates the effect of the treatment being studied.
questions.explanation: Random assignment: randomly assigning subjects to treatment groups balances out lurking variables between groups. Replication: using enough subjects per treatment group reduces the role of chance variation, making real treatment effects easier to detect. Control: keeping other variables constant across groups (e.g. a comparison/control group, placebo, or blinding) isolates the effect of the treatment being studied.

questions.q: A study testing a new fertilizer randomly assigns 60 plants to fertilizer or no-fertilizer groups, but only uses 3 plants per group. Identify the design flaw, and explain the consequence.
questions.target: The three principles of experimental design (RRCB)
questions.answer: The flaw is insufficient replication: with only 3 plants per group, natural plant-to-plant variation could easily produce an apparent difference between groups purely by chance, making it hard to distinguish a real fertilizer effect from random variability.
questions.explanation: The flaw is insufficient replication: with only 3 plants per group, natural plant-to-plant variation could easily produce an apparent difference between groups purely by chance, making it hard to distinguish a real fertilizer effect from random variability.

questions.q: A study on a new medication expects men and women to respond differently. Describe how a randomized block design would be set up, using sex as the blocking variable.
questions.answer: Separate the subjects into two blocks by sex (men and women), then randomly assign subjects to treatment or control within each block separately. This ensures the medication is compared fairly within each sex group, removing sex as a source of confounding variation between the treatment and control groups.
questions.explanation: Separate the subjects into two blocks by sex (men and women), then randomly assign subjects to treatment or control within each block separately. This ensures the medication is compared fairly within each sex group, removing sex as a source of confounding variation between the treatment and control groups.

questions.q: A researcher wants to compare two brands of running shoes on the same 20 runners, having each runner test both brands (in random order) and comparing their times. Identify this design.
questions.answer: This is a matched pairs design (a special case of blocking where each subject serves as their own block), since each runner is compared to themselves under both treatments rather than to a different group of runners.
questions.explanation: This is a matched pairs design (a special case of blocking where each subject serves as their own block), since each runner is compared to themselves under both treatments rather than to a different group of runners.

questions.q: Explain what the placebo effect is, and describe how a single-blind experiment design controls for it.
questions.answer: The placebo effect is an improvement in a subject's condition simply because they believe they are receiving a treatment, even if the treatment has no active effect. A single-blind design controls for this by giving the control group a placebo that looks identical to the real treatment, so subjects do not know which group they are in, ensuring the psychological effect of expecting treatment applies equally to both groups.
questions.explanation: The placebo effect is an improvement in a subject's condition simply because they believe they are receiving a treatment, even if the treatment has no active effect. A single-blind design controls for this by giving the control group a placebo that looks identical to the real treatment, so subjects do not know which group they are in, ensuring the psychological effect of expecting treatment applies equally to both groups.

sections.heading: Part II — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Intermediate Multi-Step Application (8–14)

questions.q: Explain the difference between a single-blind and a double-blind experiment.
questions.answer: In a single-blind experiment, only the subjects are unaware of which treatment they are receiving. In a double-blind experiment, neither the subjects nor the people evaluating or administering the treatment (who might otherwise unconsciously bias their assessment) know which group is which, further reducing bias.
questions.explanation: In a single-blind experiment, only the subjects are unaware of which treatment they are receiving. In a double-blind experiment, neither the subjects nor the people evaluating or administering the treatment (who might otherwise unconsciously bias their assessment) know which group is which, further reducing bias.

questions.q: A study uses a simple random sample from the population but is purely observational (no random assignment of treatment). State what type of conclusion (about the population, about causation, both, or neither) is justified, and explain why.
questions.answer: Random sampling (without random assignment) justifies generalizing results to the population the sample was drawn from, but since there was no random assignment of a treatment, causal conclusions are not justified — only an association can be claimed for that population.
questions.explanation: Random sampling (without random assignment) justifies generalizing results to the population the sample was drawn from, but since there was no random assignment of a treatment, causal conclusions are not justified — only an association can be claimed for that population.

questions.q: A study randomly assigns treatments to a group of volunteers who were not randomly selected from any larger population. State what type of conclusion is justified.
questions.answer: Random assignment (without random sampling) justifies a causal conclusion about the effect of the treatment on the specific subjects studied, but since the volunteers were not randomly selected from a broader population, the results cannot be safely generalized beyond the study's own subjects.
questions.explanation: Random assignment (without random sampling) justifies a causal conclusion about the effect of the treatment on the specific subjects studied, but since the volunteers were not randomly selected from a broader population, the results cannot be safely generalized beyond the study's own subjects.

questions.q: A pharmaceutical company recruits 300 volunteers (not randomly selected from the general population) and randomly assigns them to receive either a new drug or a placebo, in a double-blind design. Evaluate what conclusions can and cannot be drawn from this study.
questions.target: Putting it together: evaluating a study design
questions.answer: Because subjects were randomly assigned to drug or placebo, a causal conclusion about the drug's effect (relative to placebo) on these subjects is justified — including that the double-blind design controls for the placebo effect and evaluator bias. However, because the 300 volunteers were not randomly selected from the general population, the results cannot be safely generalized to the population at large; the study only supports causal claims about the volunteers themselves (or, with caution, people similar to them).
questions.explanation: Because subjects were randomly assigned to drug or placebo, a causal conclusion about the drug's effect (relative to placebo) on these subjects is justified — including that the double-blind design controls for the placebo effect and evaluator bias. However, because the 300 volunteers were not randomly selected from the general population, the results cannot be safely generalized to the population at large; the study only supports causal claims about the volunteers themselves (or, with caution, people similar to them).

questions.q: An observational study finds that people who drink more coffee have a higher rate of heart disease. Explain how smoking could act as a confounding variable in this relationship.
questions.answer: If people who drink a lot of coffee are also more likely to smoke, and smoking independently increases the risk of heart disease, then smoking is a confounding variable: it is associated with both coffee drinking and heart disease, making it impossible to tell from this observational data alone whether coffee itself, smoking, or some combination is responsible for the observed relationship.
questions.explanation: If people who drink a lot of coffee are also more likely to smoke, and smoking independently increases the risk of heart disease, then smoking is a confounding variable: it is associated with both coffee drinking and heart disease, making it impossible to tell from this observational data alone whether coffee itself, smoking, or some combination is responsible for the observed relationship.

questions.q: Explain how a well-designed randomized experiment would help rule out a variable like smoking as a confounder in the coffee and heart disease example.
questions.answer: In a randomized experiment, subjects would be randomly assigned to a coffee-drinking treatment or a control group. Random assignment tends to balance the two groups on other characteristics, including smoking habits, on average — so any difference in heart disease outcomes between the groups could more confidently be attributed to coffee itself, not to smoking or other confounders that random assignment has balanced out.
questions.explanation: In a randomized experiment, subjects would be randomly assigned to a coffee-drinking treatment or a control group. Random assignment tends to balance the two groups on other characteristics, including smoking habits, on average — so any difference in heart disease outcomes between the groups could more confidently be attributed to coffee itself, not to smoking or other confounders that random assignment has balanced out.

questions.q: A researcher tests three different fertilizer amounts (low, medium, high) on tomato plants, measuring final yield. Identify the experimental units, the treatment, and the response variable.
questions.answer: Experimental units: the individual tomato plants. Treatment: the fertilizer amount applied (low, medium, or high) — this is the explanatory variable being manipulated. Response variable: the final yield of each plant, which is measured as the outcome.
questions.explanation: Experimental units: the individual tomato plants. Treatment: the fertilizer amount applied (low, medium, or high) — this is the explanatory variable being manipulated. Response variable: the final yield of each plant, which is measured as the outcome.

sections.heading: Part III — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Challenging & Cross-Lesson Synthesis (15–20)

questions.q: A pharmaceutical researcher is testing whether a new sleep aid reduces the time it takes people to fall asleep, and worries that people with severe insomnia might respond very differently from people with mild insomnia. Design a study using a randomized block design that accounts for this concern, describing each step, and explain the specific benefit this design provides over a simple completely randomized design in this scenario.
questions.answer: First, classify each subject into a block based on insomnia severity (e.g. "mild" and "severe"). Then, within each block separately, randomly assign subjects to receive either the new sleep aid or a placebo. This ensures the comparison between sleep aid and placebo happens fairly within each severity group, rather than risking, by chance, that a completely randomized design places most severe-insomnia subjects into just one of the two treatment groups — blocking removes insomnia severity as a source of confounding, isolating the sleep aid's true effect more precisely.
questions.explanation: First, classify each subject into a block based on insomnia severity (e.g. "mild" and "severe"). Then, within each block separately, randomly assign subjects to receive either the new sleep aid or a placebo. This ensures the comparison between sleep aid and placebo happens fairly within each severity group, rather than risking, by chance, that a completely randomized design places most severe-insomnia subjects into just one of the two treatment groups — blocking removes insomnia severity as a source of confounding, isolating the sleep aid's true effect more precisely.

questions.q: A company tests a new website design by randomly assigning visitors to see either the old design or the new design, without telling visitors which version is the "experimental" one, and measures the percentage who complete a purchase. Explain why this study can support a causal conclusion about the website redesign, and describe the specific scope (which population) that conclusion applies to.
questions.answer: Because visitors are randomly assigned to see the old or new design, random assignment balances out any other differences between the two groups of visitors on average, so a difference in purchase completion rates can be causally attributed to the website design itself. However, the causal conclusion applies specifically to the population of visitors who came to this particular website during the study period — generalizing to a broader population (e.g. all internet shoppers everywhere) would require that these visitors be a representative sample of that broader population, which is not established just by the random assignment of treatment.
questions.explanation: Because visitors are randomly assigned to see the old or new design, random assignment balances out any other differences between the two groups of visitors on average, so a difference in purchase completion rates can be causally attributed to the website design itself. However, the causal conclusion applies specifically to the population of visitors who came to this particular website during the study period — generalizing to a broader population (e.g. all internet shoppers everywhere) would require that these visitors be a representative sample of that broader population, which is not established just by the random assignment of treatment.

questions.q: A university studies whether a new tutoring program improves final exam scores. Volunteers who sign up for tutoring are compared to students who did not sign up, without any random assignment. At the end of the semester, tutored students score noticeably higher on average. Explain why this study cannot establish that the tutoring program caused the improvement, identifying a specific plausible confounding variable.
questions.answer: Since students self-selected into the tutoring group rather than being randomly assigned, the tutored and non-tutored groups may differ in other important ways besides tutoring itself — for example, students motivated enough to seek out extra tutoring may also be more diligent, better organized, or more academically engaged in general (a plausible confounding variable: student motivation/effort). This makes it impossible to separate the effect of tutoring itself from the effect of the underlying motivation that led students to sign up for it in the first place, so only an association, not causation, can be claimed.
questions.explanation: Since students self-selected into the tutoring group rather than being randomly assigned, the tutored and non-tutored groups may differ in other important ways besides tutoring itself — for example, students motivated enough to seek out extra tutoring may also be more diligent, better organized, or more academically engaged in general (a plausible confounding variable: student motivation/effort). This makes it impossible to separate the effect of tutoring itself from the effect of the underlying motivation that led students to sign up for it in the first place, so only an association, not causation, can be claimed.

questions.q: An agronomist wants to test whether a new organic fertilizer increases tomato yield compared to a standard commercial fertilizer. Explain how the agronomist must incorporate the four principles of experimental design: Comparison, Random Assignment, Control, and Replication.
questions.target: The three principles of experimental design (RRCB)
questions.answer: 1. Comparison: Use two treatment groups (organic fertilizer vs. standard fertilizer control) grown concurrently under the same environmental conditions. 2. Random Assignment: Assign tomato plants to fertilizer treatments using a random number generator to balance unmeasured variables (e.g. baseline soil nutrient variations, microclimates). 3. Control: Keep all extraneous variables identical for both groups: sunlight exposure, watering schedule, soil volume, and pest control. 4. Replication: Apply each fertilizer to a large number of plants (e.g. 50 plants per treatment) so that genuine yield differences can be distinguished from natural plant-to-plant variation.
questions.explanation: 1. Comparison: Use two treatment groups (organic fertilizer vs. standard fertilizer control) grown concurrently under the same environmental conditions. 2. Random Assignment: Assign tomato plants to fertilizer treatments using a random number generator to balance unmeasured variables (e.g. baseline soil nutrient variations, microclimates). 3. Control: Keep all extraneous variables identical for both groups: sunlight exposure, watering schedule, soil volume, and pest control. 4. Replication: Apply each fertilizer to a large number of plants (e.g. 50 plants per treatment) so that genuine yield differences can be distinguished from natural plant-to-plant variation.

questions.q: A health study surveys 5,000 adults and finds that people who sleep 8 hours per night have significantly lower blood pressure than those who sleep 5 hours. (a) Can researchers conclude that increasing sleep causes a reduction in blood pressure? (b) Delineate the scope of inference using the 2×2 selection/assignment matrix.
questions.answer: (a) Causal Inference: No, cause-and-effect cannot be established because this is an observational study where sleep duration was not randomly assigned. Plausible confounding variables (e.g. job stress, diet, exercise) are associated with sleep duration and independently affect blood pressure. (b) Scope of Inference:Were individuals randomly selected from the adult population? Yes $\Rightarrow$ Inferences can be generalized to the broader adult population.Were treatments randomly assigned? No $\Rightarrow$ Inferences are strictly limited to association, NOT causation.
questions.explanation: (a) Causal Inference: No, cause-and-effect cannot be established because this is an observational study where sleep duration was not randomly assigned. Plausible confounding variables (e.g. job stress, diet, exercise) are associated with sleep duration and independently affect blood pressure. (b) Scope of Inference:Were individuals randomly selected from the adult population? Yes $\Rightarrow$ Inferences can be generalized to the broader adult population.Were treatments randomly assigned? No $\Rightarrow$ Inferences are strictly limited to association, NOT causation.

questions.q: Level 3 · AdvancedAn investigator conducts a hypothesis test at significance level $\alpha = 0.05$. Explain two distinct ways the investigator could increase the statistical power of the test without changing the true effect size.
questions.answer: 1. Increase the sample size $n$: A larger sample size reduces the standard error of the sample statistic ($\sigma / \sqrt{n}$), making the sampling distributions of $H_0$ and $H_a$ narrower, which increases the probability of rejecting a false null hypothesis (power = $1 - \beta$). 2. Increase the significance level $\alpha$ (e.g., from 0.05 to 0.10): A larger $\alpha$ moves the critical rejection boundary closer to the center of $H_0$, making it easier to reject $H_0$ and thereby increasing power (at the expense of increasing the risk of a Type I error).
questions.explanation: 1. Increase the sample size $n$: A larger sample size reduces the standard error of the sample statistic ($\sigma / \sqrt{n}$), making the sampling distributions of $H_0$ and $H_a$ narrower, which increases the probability of rejecting a false null hypothesis (power = $1 - \beta$). 2. Increase the significance level $\alpha$ (e.g., from 0.05 to 0.10): A larger $\alpha$ moves the critical rejection boundary closer to the center of $H_0$, making it easier to reject $H_0$ and thereby increasing power (at the expense of increasing the risk of a Type I error).

questions.q: In a study testing a new fertilizer, subjects do not know whether they are receiving the real treatment or a placebo, but the researchers evaluating the results do know which group each subject is in. Identify the blinding used.
questions.answer: Single-blind. Only the subjects are unaware of their group assignment, while the evaluators know — this is single-blind.

questions.q: In a study testing a new fertilizer, neither the subjects nor the researchers evaluating the results know which subjects received the real treatment versus a placebo. Identify the blinding used.
questions.answer: Double-blind. Both the subjects and the evaluators are unaware of group assignment — this is double-blind.
